tells: A specific conceptual thread of cosmic forms rhyming with earthly ones: a crater pooling a nebula, a nautilus shell (logarithmic spiral) echoing a protoplanetary disk, a human iris resolving into the Helix nebula.
The light and texture are real: macro sand with shallow depth of field, rim-lit translucent shell, volumetric dust in the accretion disk, and wet crater rock.
The type is restrained but deliberate. Wide-tracked COSMOS letters are split around the pupil so the eye becomes the 'O', and the small credits sit carefully in the negative space of each shot.
Every frame works as a poster, and the warm/cool palette resolves in the final iris/nebula frame.
The frames show choreography: scale moves from geologic to galactic to human and back.
gaps: The eye/nebula end card is a famous image and a little expected as a payoff. A final turn could surprise more.
The credit typography is functional and small; it could interact more with the subject matter.
Some cosmic shots (the accretion disk) sit near the genre's standard VFX vocabulary; push their art direction as far as the shell and crater shots go.

defects: Dead air: the ice-retreat section is one 12.5 s take, and in the 1/6 s pairs almost nothing moves, so the frame reads as a slow dissolve with no animated event
In the pairs, the 1990 and 3.57 numerals only change in opacity or mask between frames. There is no spacing, easing or follow-through to read, so nothing has weight
The bar chart builds left to right one bar at a time, so the frame sits half-empty for a long time. It reads as a reveal from a chart template, not choreography
Small top-left captions sit straight on top of the high-contrast crack pattern. 'September 2011: 4.56' is partly broken up by the cracks and hard to read
The 2012/3.57 highlight is a flat orange fill on bars that are otherwise textured with ice. The material rule breaks at the most important data point
The chart's '1979 level' hairline and axis labels are very thin and small at 1080p and will shimmer or vanish when compressed
The Greenland end card is stacked statically on the right. The overlay is placed, not animated into the ice field, so the payoff arrives as a still
gaps: Motion: the strong idea (the stencil years being eaten as the ice breaks up, the 2012 record low, a Greenland-sized hole) is shown in slow, linear crossfades. Top studios would give the ice physical behaviour: floes cracking on a beat, drifting with inertia and overshoot, and the numeral fragments sinking with weight. They would also cut the 12.5 s and 4.4 s holds down to a living rhythm of about 2.5 s

Arc and transitions: energy stays flat and then decays. The year-to-year handoffs are dissolves, not match-cuts. The ice could morph into the bars and the bars could break back into floes around Greenland, building to a clear peak at 2012 before the release

Sound: a sustained harmonic drone with only three transient hits (about 4.2 s, 13.1 s and 18 s) and one noise swell. The arrangement is static, with no cracking, water or foley sound design tied to individual floes, and little dynamic shape apart from the swell at 24–26 s
